meta.title: Selene DB 2.0 Final Implementation Plan
meta.line_in_sand: 1.x is EOL; no maintenance, compatibility, reader, or migration.
meta.machine_role: Portable mirror of the reviewed plan; Markdown is the human review surface.

milestones.title: 2.0 Pivot, 1.x End-of-Life, Governance, and Baselines
milestones.objective: Create an irreversible and auditable line between the prototype-era 1.x series and the active 2.0 program before architectural code begins.
rationale: The current development branch contains substantial unreleased work, but the user has explicitly chosen a breaking 2.0 pivot rather than a 1.5 release.
Branch, release, support, review, and evidence rules must be changed before agents begin broad refactors, otherwise later PRs can accidentally preserve obsolete contracts.
A fresh executable baseline is required because the architecture review was source-based and did not independently run the workspace gates.
entry: Confirm `b8782bec34ff0b815b62711ac7e33cac09d8ea71` is still the intended 1.x archival source snapshot.
Confirm no active customer or internal deployment requires a 1.x patch stream or persisted-format migration.
Ensure repository owner can create a protected archive branch and annotated non-release tag.
decisions: 1.x becomes end-of-life immediately: no maintenance, security, compatibility, or release promises remain.
Archive source at branch `archive/1.x-final` and tag `archive-v1-eol-2026-08-21`; the tag intentionally does not match the release workflow pattern `v*.*.*`.
`development` becomes the sole 2.0 integration branch and workspace packages move to `2.0.0-alpha.1`.
`main` may remain the last published 1.x release line until 2.0 GA, but it is archival rather than maintained.
Implementers edit and test only; orchestrators own Git history, non-draft PR mutations, consolidated independent-review comments, and eligible authorized merges under D-022.
exit: Repository-facing EOL language is unambiguous and repeated in README, CHANGELOG, contributing/agent guidance, and 2.0 docs.
The version/branch/release policy cannot accidentally publish a 1.x or pre-release archive tag.
The 2.0 plan, review protocol, baseline, and known-risk ledger are committed and linked from repository documentation.
The complete baseline gate has been run on the pinned source, with failures and benchmark provenance recorded rather than normalized away.
risks: Creating a semver-shaped archive tag can trigger crates.io publication.
Bumping every workspace package without checking intra-workspace version pins can leave a mixed-version graph.
A docs-only declaration without branch and CI enforcement can be ignored by later agents.
Baseline failures may uncover a prerequisite defect; do not hide those defects inside the pivot PR.
iso_anchors: Repository release and support policy; no normative ISO behavior change

milestones.title: Executable GQL Conformance Profile and Evidence System
milestones.objective: Replace the hand-maintained feature and Annex B ledgers with one generated, implication-closed source of truth that controls claims, flagging, documentation, and tests.
rationale: The current feature register contains high-confidence implication conflicts and cannot safely support a formal minimum-conformance statement.
Implementation-defined IDs are part of the implementation claim, and the current Annex B mapping includes at least one direct mismatch for IA001.
Building the evidence system first prevents later catalog, session, type, and path work from creating another disconnected claim ledger.
entry: M00 EOL and repository governance are merged.
The licensed ISO document remains local reference material and is not copied into the repository.
The team accepts that the release claim is evidence-gated and may remain “ISO-aligned” until the generated gate is green.
decisions: Add a leaf `selene-profile` crate and checked-in machine-readable profile data; it must not depend on engine crates.
Every supported feature must include the transitive closure of Table 10 implied features.
Every applicable implementation-defined element has an explicit value, rationale, evidence link, and release visibility.
Generated artifacts are deterministic and checked in; hand edits to generated output fail CI.
The initial target is a named Selene core profile, not an unsupported blanket claim to all optional GQL features.
exit: Feature, implication, Annex B, Unicode, extension, and evidence registries are generated from one source.
Current conflicting claims are either withdrawn or backed by scheduled implementation dependencies.
Parser flagging, runtime feature reporting, docs, and release manifests consume the generated profile.
A release claim gate can answer exactly which rule or evidence item blocks a claim.
risks: Reproducing copyrighted normative prose instead of recording identifiers and paraphrased implementation decisions.
Encoding only direct implications while missing transitive closure or cycles.
Treating “implemented” as equivalent to “conformant” without positive, negative, and status-code evidence.
Letting runtime and documentation load different generated versions.

milestones.title: Database Facade and Catalog Ownership
milestones.objective: Move the public ownership root from one `SharedGraph` to an embedded `Database` whose catalog owns schemas, named graphs, graph types, procedures, constraints, and indexes.
rationale: ISO GQL is organized around an environment, catalog, schema, and request execution context, while the current library binds sessions directly to one graph.
A stable facade is needed before lower crates can be aggressively reshaped without repeatedly breaking embedders.
Named graph management closes a central conformance dependency and provides the ownership boundary for later transactions and persistence.
entry: The EOL policy explicitly permits removal of direct 1.x construction and session APIs.
The catalog scope decision is locked: one synthetic root directory, multiple schemas, no child directories in 2.0.
The implementation remains embedded and in-process; no server, wire protocol, or bundled authentication service is added.
decisions: Add `selene-catalog` for descriptors and `selene-db` as the only stability-promised facade crate.
Use persistent opaque catalog object IDs distinct from user-visible canonical names.
Represent the catalog root as a single directory that contains schemas only; profile IL020 is fixed accordingly and nested directories are deferred.
A `Database` owns the catalog registry, graph instances, store authority, native procedure catalog, and conformance profile.
Lower crates remain available to advanced internal users only when explicitly re-exported; no blanket stability promise applies.
exit: An embedder can create/open a `Database`, create schemas and graphs, open a session, and execute against a named graph without constructing `SharedGraph` directly.
Catalog descriptors have durable IDs, canonical names, parent ownership, object kind, and generation metadata.
GQL `CREATE/DROP SCHEMA`, `CREATE/DROP GRAPH`, and `CREATE/DROP GRAPH TYPE` resolve through the same catalog service as Rust APIs.
Old graph-root quickstarts and public entry points are removed rather than wrapped indefinitely.
risks: Putting graph storage objects directly inside catalog descriptor types and creating dependency cycles.
Leaking `Arc<SharedGraph>` as the facade contract and thereby recreating the old ownership root.
Implementing nested directory traversal before the flat catalog is proven.
Giving Rust and GQL DDL separate validation or publication paths.

milestones.title: Session, Request, Execution, and Transaction Semantics
milestones.objective: Implement explicit ISO-shaped context and outcome objects so every request has deterministic schema, graph, parameter, transaction, diagnostic, and result semantics.
rationale: The current `Session` lifetime and one-graph binding cannot express catalog navigation or consecutive requests over multiple graphs.
Session, request, execution, and transaction state are distinct concepts in the standard and should not be collapsed into executor-local structs.
A formal context model is required before compiler annotation and plan caching can be made catalog-aware.
entry: Database/catalog identity and named graph lifecycle are merged.
The implementation-defined profile has fields for default time zone, match mode, session parameters, principal behavior, and result-type exposure.
A single-owner, allow-all local policy is acceptable as the default, while an embedder-supplied authorization provider remains possible.
decisions: Sessions own an `Arc<DatabaseInner>` and persist state across requests without borrowing one graph.
Request parameters shadow session parameters by name and are type checked before execution.
Execution contexts carry immutable working records/tables and structured outcomes rather than ad hoc error/result pairs.
At most one active serializable transaction exists per session; explicit and implicit demarcation share one state machine.
Catalog and data mutations use one atomic transaction publication boundary once persistence lands.
exit: Session set/reset/close and working schema/graph selection are testable across consecutive requests.
Successful, omitted, no-data, warning, and failed outcomes preserve declared type and diagnostic bundles according to profile policy.
Explicit START/COMMIT/ROLLBACK and implicit auto-commit produce equivalent state transitions where required.
No request can outlive its session or observe a graph/catalog generation it was not analyzed against without a typed replan/retry outcome.
risks: Mixing transport connection concepts into the embedded session API.
Allowing a session mutation to leak through a failed request.
Conflating Rust panics or I/O errors with GQL conditions without preserving both layers.
Caching plans without session schema/graph/profile/catalog generation dependencies.

milestones.title: Stable Identity, Typed Candidate Sets, and Mixed Edge Directionality
milestones.objective: Make physical row space impossible to misuse through public APIs and add explicit directed/undirected edge semantics across storage, traversal, type validation, and change events.
rationale: Open issue #1093 demonstrates that bare row-indexed bitmaps defeat the purpose of the `RowIndex` newtype at the public boundary.
The ISO graph model permits directed, undirected, and mixed graphs, while current storage is effectively directed-only.
Identity and directionality decisions affect query planning, path semantics, indexes, persistence records, and reference values and therefore must precede those rewrites.
entry: Named graph and catalog object identity is merged and available through the new database facade.
The session root no longer borrows a single `SharedGraph`; graph selection is catalog-resolved.
The team accepts removal of every public API that returns untyped row-space data.
Logical identity and directionality records may be introduced now, while byte-level format 2.0 remains deferred to M09.
decisions: External node/edge IDs remain stable and monotonic; compaction may remap private rows.
Candidate sets may use row bitmaps internally but are graph-, generation-, and element-kind bound.
Mixed graphs are the physical model; directed-only and undirected-only graph types are constraints over that model.
No 1.x persisted edge encoding is retained in the 2.0 runtime.
exit: All public enumeration and index APIs yield IDs, typed handles, or `CandidateSet<Node/Edge>` rather than raw `RoaringBitmap`/`u32` rows.
Set algebra refuses cross-graph, cross-generation, or cross-kind operations with typed errors.
Edges carry explicit directionality and endpoint semantics, including loops and canonical undirected endpoint representation.
Traversal and pattern matching distinguish edge directionality from path orientation.
Change events and logical snapshot records can represent mixed edges without format ambiguity.
risks: Exposing a conversion method that still lets callers manufacture IDs from rows.
Using endpoint ordering as semantic direction for undirected edges.
Forgetting secondary surfaces such as algorithms projections, candidate state, indexes, verification, and procedures.
Changing identity generation and directionality in one unreviewable mega-PR.

milestones.title: Semantic Compiler and Logical GQL IR
milestones.objective: Separate source syntax, annotated semantics, logical algebra, and diagnostics so catalog resolution and GQL rules are explicit before physical planning.
rationale: The current parse/analyze/plan layers are valuable, but the plan representation still mixes semantic and physical concerns.
Catalog-aware references, structural type descriptors, effect classification, and working graph/schema semantics need a stable compiler contract.
A typed logical plan is the bridge between conformance rules and the new batch/path engines.
entry: Catalog descriptors, named graph resolution, and explicit session/request contexts are merged.
Stable node/edge/reference identity and mixed-edge semantic types are available to the analyzer.
The generated conformance profile is the only authority for feature and implementation-defined behavior.
The current parser corpus and analyzed-plan snapshots have a recorded baseline for differential work.
decisions: The parser remains a strict GQL syntax parser; no SQL/Cypher/SPARQL aliases are introduced.
The syntax AST preserves source spelling and spans but does not carry mutable resolution state.
The annotated semantic tree is immutable and references catalog/profile/context snapshots by stable IDs and generations.
Logical plans describe GQL binding-table and graph semantics without choosing concrete row/bitmap/index algorithms.
exit: Every name, parameter, graph reference, property reference, variable, and procedure call has a resolved semantic descriptor or a structured diagnostic.
Type/nullability/degree-of-reference and effect metadata are complete before lowering.
Logical operators cover query, catalog mutation, data mutation, procedure, and transaction categories.
Golden snapshots and deterministic IDs make analyzer/planner drift reviewable.
The old mixed execution plan is isolated behind a temporary bridge with a scheduled deletion PR.
risks: Adding physical index or row-layout fields to logical operators.
Letting optimizer rewrites alter declared result types or diagnostics.
Using string names after semantic resolution where stable IDs are available.
Rewriting the parser and semantic compiler simultaneously without snapshot parity evidence.

milestones.title: Physical Planning and Batch-Oriented Execution
milestones.objective: Replace the row-at-a-time executor with a typed batch engine while preserving low-latency embedded use and exact GQL binding-table semantics.
rationale: The current row-at-a-time runtime is a performance and architecture ceiling for joins, grouping, expression evaluation, vectors, text, and path results.
Research on vectorized query engines shows batch processing reduces interpretation overhead, while selection vectors and bitmaps have workload-dependent strengths.
A separate physical plan allows algorithm choices to change without mutating semantic analysis or conformance evidence.
entry: A typed logical plan exists for every statement category that will enter the new executor.
Public row-space leakage has been removed or isolated behind an internal compatibility bridge.
The row-at-a-time executor has an explicit oracle role and differential corpus rather than an open-ended coexistence promise.
Baseline latency, scan, join, grouping, and allocation rows are recorded before execution changes.
decisions: Use a pull-based `next_batch` operator protocol with bounded batches; async execution is not introduced.
A batch carries a binding-table descriptor, immutable columns, cardinality, and an explicit active-row representation.
Selection vectors are the default sparse survivor representation; bitmaps remain available for SIMD-friendly/index-native operations.
The row executor is a temporary oracle/bridge only and is deleted before milestone exit.
exit: Scan, filter, project, join, group, sort, page, mutation, DDL, transaction, and procedure operators execute through the physical plan.
Batch and row oracle outputs are differential-tested over the existing positive/negative corpus during transition.
Result ordering, duplicates, nulls, record types, preferred column order, and status propagation match logical semantics.
Performance gates cover one-row latency, medium scans, joins, grouping, and memory amplification.
No public API exposes executor-internal column or row indices.
risks: Designing a full code generator/JIT before a batch interpreter exists.
Materializing every operator boundary and losing streaming behavior.
Converting all values to one boxed representation and masking CPU gains with allocation.
Deleting the old executor before differential coverage reaches all supported statement categories.
iso_anchors: Clause 22 binding, join, grouping, equality, and ordering semantics

milestones.title: GQL Path Pattern and Selective Search Engine
milestones.objective: Implement path expressions as explicit automata over mixed property graphs, with finite-result guarantees, path modes, match modes, selective search, and compact path values.
rationale: Path semantics are a defining GQL capability and one of the hardest areas to validate through ad hoc traversal code.
The standard models path pattern expressions as regular-language machinery with explicit walk/trail/simple/acyclic and selective-search behavior.
Recent graph-query research supports automaton/product-graph evaluation, algebraic execution, and compact shared path representations for large intermediate sets.
entry: Mixed directed/undirected edge semantics and stable graph-element references are merged.
Path syntax and degree-of-reference information are represented in the annotated semantic tree and logical IR.
The batch engine can stream typed binding tables and can host a dedicated path operator without exposing physical rows.
A simple exhaustive small-graph path oracle and corpus format are agreed before optimized traversal begins.
decisions: Lower path syntax to a semantic automaton independent of traversal strategy.
Execute against a graph-product state space that includes automaton state, node, and mode-specific visitation state.
Finite-result guards are enforced during analysis and planning rather than by arbitrary runtime caps.
Full path values are supported; compact internal representation must remain semantically invisible.
Performance specializations are evidence-gated and must preserve a simple reference evaluator.
exit: Bounded patterns, quantified patterns, alternation, concatenation, parenthesized terms, and label/where constraints have explicit IR and tests.
WALK, TRAIL, SIMPLE, ACYCLIC, DIFFERENT EDGES, and REPEATABLE ELEMENTS produce exact reference-equivalent results.
ANY, ALL SHORTEST, counted shortest, and counted shortest-group selection are partitioned by endpoints as required.
Path variables and path values preserve element order, edge orientation, and reference validity.
Differential small-graph enumeration and targeted LDBC-style benchmarks gate optimization.
risks: Treating undirected traversal as two stored directed edges and duplicating identity.
Applying global shortest selection instead of endpoint-partitioned selection.
Using a path cap to hide an infinite-result semantic error.
Adopting a compact path representation without deterministic enumeration and reference equality tests.

milestones.title: Catalog-Owned Constraints, Expression Indexes, JSON Paths, and Storage Performance
milestones.objective: Unify integrity constraints and indexes under catalog ownership, make uniqueness incremental and composite, add deterministic expression indexes, and deliberately settle read-hot storage representations.
rationale: Open issues #1092 and #1094 show that uniqueness declaration and enforcement are separated from existing composite index machinery.
Open issue #1097 identifies JSON scalar-path lookup as the highest-value expression-index use case.
Open issue #1137 demonstrates that storage map choices need balanced read/write evidence and section-level baseline provenance.
entry: Catalog descriptor ownership and transaction-visible graph snapshots are merged.
Typed candidate sets and generation checks are available for index access paths.
Semantic scalar-expression descriptors and physical scan/filter operators exist.
Current uniqueness, index drift, JSON scan, and read/write benchmark behavior has been captured before replacement.
decisions: Indexes and constraints are catalog descriptors with stable IDs, lifecycle state, target expressions, and backing-state metadata.
Single-property uniqueness is the arity-one case of a named tuple constraint.
A uniqueness/key constraint requires a usable backing index; the engine creates or binds one transactionally instead of scanning every commit.
Expression index targets are deterministic, side-effect-free, catalog-resolved scalar expressions over one element.
JSON scalar-path indexes reuse typed scalar index structures; GIN-style containment indexes are deferred.
Storage collection choices are per-map decisions backed by isolated read and write A/B data.
exit: Composite unique constraints are declarable for node and edge types and use typed tuple encoding without separator ambiguity.
Incremental validation probes transaction-visible backing indexes and remains race-free under the single-writer boundary.
Expression indexes are maintained on create/update/delete, replay, recovery, compaction, and schema change.
The optimizer matches semantically equivalent JSON path expressions to registered targets.
Read-hot map regressions are resolved or explicitly accepted with weighted workload evidence and permanent guard rows.
risks: Equating GQL key label sets with every native uniqueness constraint without documenting the extension boundary.
Letting an index silently decline probes while a constraint assumes completeness.
Allowing nondeterministic functions, parameters, procedures, or cross-element references in index expressions.
Optimizing only steady-state reads and ignoring clone/mutation/recovery cost.
iso_anchors: Clause 4.13.2 graph element types and key label sets

milestones.title: Persistence Authority, WAL, Snapshot, and Recovery Format 2.0
milestones.objective: Establish one anchored filesystem and durability authority, implement explicit written/flushed/published/acknowledged commit phases, and cut over to a new 2.0-only persisted format.
rationale: Open issue #1088 identifies pathname re-resolution as a correctness boundary that cannot be solved by caller preflight checks.
Open issue #1128 shows the current writer lacks a flushed watermark and therefore over-reports indeterminate outcomes.
Catalog-first ownership, mixed edges, constraints, and multiple named graphs require a new logical durable record model and snapshot layout.
entry: Database/catalog ownership, transaction semantics, graph identity, mixed edges, and catalog object descriptors are stable enough to encode.
Constraint and index descriptors have stable logical forms, even when derived accelerator bytes remain rebuildable.
The final 1.x archival source has been protected and the no-migration policy is already public.
A crash/fault-injection matrix and platform filesystem test strategy are approved before any format is declared authoritative.
decisions: A `StoreDirectory` capability is opened once and all managed artifact operations are relative to it.
Exactly one commit-critical WAL is authoritative; vector/text/JSON/algorithm accelerators are rebuildable observers unless a future ADR changes that.
Commit phases are `validate → encode/append → flush → publish → acknowledge` with explicit watermarks and failure classes.
The 2.0 runtime writes and reads only format 2.0. It may inspect a small header to return a typed 1.x unsupported-format error, but it includes no 1.x decoder or migration path.
Catalog and graph data share transaction and recovery epochs.
exit: Rename/replacement tests prove all WAL, manifest, lock, snapshot, archive, and temporary operations stay under the anchored directory.
Written, flushed, published, and acknowledged positions are monotonic and crash-tested; rollback/cancel versus unknown outcomes are precise.
Checksummed segment framing distinguishes provable tail tears from interior corruption without destructive repair.
Snapshot/MANIFEST/CURRENT publication, checkpoint rotation, retention, and recovery form one state machine.
Format 1.x stores fail with an actionable typed error and no files are modified.
risks: Using canonicalized paths as identity after the capability has been opened.
Treating truncation as durable without syncing the file and parent metadata where required.
Keeping multiple commit-critical providers that can disagree after partial success.
Adding a hidden 1.x replay path “temporarily” and thereby reintroducing compatibility obligations.
Publishing catalog and graph snapshots at different cuts.
iso_anchors: Implementation-defined storage/API mechanism; persisted format itself is outside GQL

milestones.title: Native Capability Reintegration, Conformance Closure, and 2.0 Release
milestones.objective: Bring algorithms, vectors, text, JSON, and procedures back through the new facade and catalog, close the selected GQL profile with executable evidence, and harden a publishable 2.0 release.
rationale: The existing native retrieval and algorithm work is valuable and should be retained, but only after the new ownership, execution, identity, and persistence contracts are stable.
A 2.0 release must state exactly what is conformant, what is a Selene extension, and what remains unsupported.
Release readiness requires system-wide crash, fuzz, mutation, benchmark, documentation, and packaging evidence rather than feature count.
entry: All preceding milestone exit gates are green at a pinned release-candidate base SHA.
No temporary legacy public API, row executor, 1.x persistence reader, or dual ownership path remains in the stability-promised facade.
The selected conformance profile and unresolved evidence gaps are visible and reviewed before release scope is frozen.
Native feature baseline tests and benchmarks are available so reintegration can distinguish wiring changes from semantic drift.
decisions: Native features are accessed through catalog descriptors and namespaced procedures; no loadable extension ABI is introduced.
Exact vector, BM25, JSON, and graph algorithms remain correctness oracles; derived accelerators are rebuildable.
The release claim is generated from the profile/evidence registry and may not be stronger than the gate result.
There is no 1.x migration promise; upgrade guidance directs users to rebuild/import from source data.
GA requires no temporary 1.x/public/executor/persistence bridge left in the stable facade.
exit: Algorithms, vector, text, JSON, index maintenance, procedures, recovery, and catalog introspection work through `selene-db` and batch execution.
The selected profile is implication-closed, all mandatory and claimed feature evidence is green, and Annex B/extension disclosures are generated.
Public API, examples, rustdoc, error handling, release notes, package metadata, and crates.io dry runs are coherent.
Full CI, fuzz, mutation, crash matrix, benchmark guard set, and cross-platform release workflows pass at the release candidate SHA.
A final independent reviewer pair returns Blocker/Major-clean PASS on the unchanged exact head before an authorized merge; tag and publication remain separately controlled.
risks: Reintroducing old graph-root APIs to make native features easier to wire.
Claiming ISO minimum conformance based on feature labels without complete evidence.
Allowing approximate retrieval paths to return unreranked or semantically different scores.
Shipping with stale benchmark dates or generated conformance artifacts.
Tagging or publishing before archive/release workflows are dry-run verified.

pull_requests.title: Declare 1.x End-of-Life and Establish the 2.0 Line
pull_requests.outcome: Make the support and version break executable: archive the final 1.x source snapshot, move the active workspace to 2.0 alpha, and remove every repository statement that implies future 1.x maintenance.
scope: Verify the working branch contains `b8782bec34ff0b815b62711ac7e33cac09d8ea71` or explicitly record and review any newer base before editing.
Bump all workspace/package versions from 1.x to `2.0.0-alpha.1` and update path dependency version constraints atomically.
Add a prominent 1.x EOL statement: no fixes, security patches, compatibility maintenance, new 1.x releases, or persisted-format migration support.
Document the owner-only archival actions for protected branch `archive/1.x-final` and annotated tag `archive-v1-eol-2026-08-21` at `b8782bec34ff0b815b62711ac7e33cac09d8ea71`.
Update release workflow comments and checks so non-semver archive tags do not publish crates and 2.0 pre-release tags are handled intentionally.
Delete or rewrite staged “1.5.0” language in release notes, plans, and agent instructions; do not silently call unreleased work a 1.5 release.
non_goals: No engine architecture or behavior change beyond version/support/release controls.
No attempt to publish 1.5.0, create a 1.x patch branch, or build a migration tool.
No source deletion from the archive snapshot; archival Git objects preserve it.
No 2.0 API design beyond links to the finalized decision document.
design: `development` is the only active 2.0 integration trunk. Feature branches target it.
`main` is not a maintained 1.x branch; it remains historical until the eventual 2.0 release PR updates it.
The archive branch/tag are immutable evidence, not supported release channels and not selected by CI publication patterns.
The new pre-release version is consistent across every publishable package and lockfile metadata.
EOL wording distinguishes “source remains available” from “support continues”.
acceptance: `cargo metadata --locked --format-version 1` shows `2.0.0-alpha.1` for all Selene workspace packages and no 1.x path dependency constraints.
A repository-wide search finds no forward-looking promise for 1.5.0 or 1.x maintenance outside historical changelog entries clearly marked historical.
README and CHANGELOG state the EOL policy in the first relevant release/support section.
Release/tag workflow tests prove `archive-v1-eol-*` is not a publish trigger and intended 2.0 tags still are.
The PR description contains the exact post-merge owner commands for archive branch/tag creation and their verification commands.
No crate API or file format compatibility shim is added.
tests: Run `cargo metadata --locked --format-version 1` and inspect package and dependency versions.
Run the repository metadata/release scripts affected by version changes.
Add or update shell tests for tag classification where the release workflow uses pattern logic.
Run `cargo check --workspace --locked` to catch mixed path-version constraints.
Run `git grep -nE "1\.5\.0|maintain(ed|ing)? 1\.x|1\.x support"` and classify every remaining match.
benchmarks: None; this is a release-governance PR. Record “not applicable” rather than running unrelated benches.
docs: Add `docs/v2/eol-and-version-policy.md` with branch/tag/version/support matrix and no-migration policy.
Update public README/CHANGELOG and contributor/agent workflow links.
review_focus: EOL wording has no exception that recreates a maintenance obligation.
Archive actions point to the exact reviewed SHA.
stop_conditions: The source SHA differs and contains unreviewed changes.
A current deployment owner requires 1.x fixes or a migration path.
The archive tag would trigger existing release automation.
Version bump exposes unrelated compile failures that cannot be isolated.
bridge: No bridge. The PR intentionally removes compatibility promises.
After merge, the repository owner creates and protects the archive branch/tag; implementers do not perform Git, GitHub, settings, release, or archive mutations.

pull_requests.title: Commit the Finalized 2.0 Architecture and Milestone Contract
pull_requests.outcome: Install the approved architecture decisions, master milestone map, PR review protocol, and issue mapping as tracked repository documentation that future agents must follow.
scope: Add the finalized decision record covering product boundary, facade, catalog scope, conformance policy, contexts, identity, edge directionality, compiler, executor, constraints/indexes, persistence, extensions, and release criteria.
Add the milestone/PR package or a repository-native copy of its canonical documents under tracked `docs/v2/` paths; underscore working directories remain untracked.
Add the PASS/FIX/REPLAN review protocol with separate implementer, orchestrator, and independent read-only reviewer roles.
Map every current open issue to its owning 2.0 PR and state that issues are closed only by the owning implementation PR.
Link 2.0 docs from README and AGENTS without turning AGENTS into a fast-moving PR ledger.
Record source snapshot, assumptions, research boundaries, and the fact that the initial review did not independently execute the Rust suite.
non_goals: No GitHub milestone/issue mutation in this PR.
No copying of the licensed ISO PDF or substantial normative text into the repository.
No re-opening finalized architecture choices without an explicit REPLAN decision.
design: `docs/v2/` is the tracked program-of-record; untracked local notes are supplementary only.
Each PR specification has one owner milestone, explicit dependencies, acceptance evidence, review focus, and stop conditions.
Architecture decisions are stable; implementation details may change only when evidence and a recorded delta justify it.
The tracker JSON/HTML is generated from the same milestone metadata where practical, but Markdown remains the reviewable source.
acceptance: All relative links in the 2.0 documentation resolve in a link-check script.
The documented milestone and PR counts match the canonical plan data.
The seven current open issues each map to exactly one owning PR.
AGENTS clearly separates implementer edit/test work from orchestrator Git, PR, review-comment, and eligible authorized merge mutations and includes the required handoff fields.
No tracked document directs future work into a gitignored underscore directory.
ISO references use clause/feature/implementation-defined IDs and paraphrase rather than reproducing the standard.
tests: Run docs-only repository gates: formatting where applicable, file-size, secret scan, doc constants/registry scripts, and `git diff --check`.
Verify generated tracker JSON schema if included.
Inspect repository search results for contradictory merge/support instructions.
benchmarks: None; documentation and governance only.
docs: This PR is the documentation installation itself.
Add a compact README link rather than duplicating the full plan in top-level files.
review_focus: Decision text matches the finalized package exactly.
No hidden optionality around 1.x support and no ambiguity in the corrected role or merge-eligibility model.
PR slices are implementation-sized rather than broad epics.
Tracked versus local working-document rules are coherent.
stop_conditions: A finalized decision conflicts with current source facts discovered during installation.
The plan would require committing licensed ISO material.
The generated package and Markdown disagree on identifiers or dependencies.
bridge: This document set supersedes the earlier high-level review roadmap for implementation sequencing.
Keep the original review notes under a research/history subsection; do not delete the evidence behind the plan.

pull_requests.title: Enforce the 2.0 PR, Review, and CI Operating Model
pull_requests.outcome: Turn the 2.0 operating model into repository automation: practical Rust checks on every non-draft development PR, deterministic plan validation, complete handoff evidence, and exact-head merge eligibility.
scope: Add a development-PR Rust compile/test lane that is bounded enough for routine work but cannot accept syntactically valid, uncompiled architecture changes.
Validate milestone/PR identifiers, dependency references, issue ownership, and generated tracker freshness.
Install a PR template requiring plan ID, scope, deviations, tests, benchmarks, bridge/deletion obligations, and handoff summary.
Document non-draft PR handling, the independent reviewer pair, exact-head merge eligibility, and the post-merge branch-protection settings action.
Keep full cross-platform, audit, fuzz, and exhaustive gates on the main/release path while defining risk-triggered gates for each PR.
Replace the blanket agent merge prohibition with the corrected implementer/orchestrator separation and explicit authorization conditions.

decisions.decision: 1.x is end-of-life immediately. No fixes, security patches, compatibility maintenance, future 1.x release, or persisted migration path.
Archive `b8782bec34ff0b815b62711ac7e33cac09d8ea71` at `archive/1.x-final` and `archive-v1-eol-2026-08-21`. The non-semver archive tag must not trigger publication.
Selene DB 2.0 remains an embedded Rust database library. A server, wire protocol, bundled auth service, distributed execution, and loadable extension ABI are out of scope.
`selene-db` is the stability-promised facade. Lower crates are internal/advanced unless explicitly re-exported and documented.
One synthetic catalog root directory contains multiple schemas and no child directories. Catalog owns graphs, graph types, procedures, constraints, and indexes.
Claims are generated and evidence-gated. The release may use “ISO/IEC 39075:2024-aligned” with exact gaps, but may not claim minimum/selected-profile conformance until the complete gate is green.
Retain serializable single-writer publication with immutable reader snapshots. No MVCC or weaker isolation in the initial 2.0 program.
Node/edge/catalog IDs are stable semantic identity. Rows are private snapshot-scoped physical positions. Public candidate sets are graph-, generation-, and kind-bound.
The physical graph is a mixed multigraph with explicit directed and undirected edge directionality and one identity per edge.
Session, request, execution, outcome, and transaction are explicit separate objects. Sessions own the database, not one borrowed graph.
The compiler pipeline is source syntax AST → immutable annotated semantic tree → logical IR → physical plan → runtime operators.
The production executor is pull-based and batch-oriented. Row execution may exist only as a test oracle during transition and is deleted before M06 exit.
Path expressions lower to automata/product-graph execution with exact mode/match/selective semantics and a permanent small-graph reference oracle.
Constraints and indexes are catalog descriptors. Unique/key constraints require complete backing indexes. Single-property uniqueness is arity one.
Index expressions are analyzed, deterministic, pure scalar expressions over one element. JSON scalar paths reuse typed scalar indexes; containment indexes are deferred.
One anchored `StoreDirectory` capability owns all artifact operations. Path wrappers anchor once and never re-resolve during the operation lifetime.
One commit-critical WAL is authoritative. Derived vector/text/JSON/algorithm structures are rebuildable observers unless a future ADR explicitly changes this.
Commit phases are validate → encode/append → flush → publish → acknowledge, with explicit written/flushed/published/acknowledged state and precise canceled/committed/indeterminate outcomes.
2.0 writes and reads only format 2. A bounded header probe may identify 1.x to return an unsupported-format error; no 1.x decoder or migration is shipped.
Algorithms, vectors, BM25/text, JSON, and native procedures return through the facade/catalog/batch system and remain namespaced extensions where not ISO features.
Default PR cap is one invariant, at most 25 production files and roughly 1,500 net non-generated lines. Exceeding the cap requires stop/replan or an explicit reviewed exception.

Implementers edit and test only. Orchestrators own Git history, non-draft PR mutations, consolidated comments from an independent read-only reviewer pair, and eligible authorized merges. Merge requires an unchanged reviewed head, green required exact-head checks, Blocker/Major-clean final review, repository-policy permission, clean scope/worktree state, and explicit user authorization; a changed head voids PASS.
